title: 5th Circuit blocks Texas law requiring websites to filter "harmful" speech
gist: The 5th Circuit ruled 2-1 that Texas's SCOPE Act cannot force social media platforms to monitor and filter content to shield minors from 'harmful' material, holding the requirement is preempted by Section 230, while leaving intact the law's age-verification, age-registration, and ad-targeting restrictions after a separate student challenge was dismissed for lack of standing.

insights.claim: The 5th Circuit ruled 2-1 that Texas's SCOPE Act requirement forcing social media platforms to monitor and filter content to prevent minors from seeing categories of 'harmful' speech (suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, substance abuse, grooming, trafficking, etc.) is preempted by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, blocking Texas from enforcing that specific provision.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Sets circuit-level precedent limiting how far state 'kid safety' laws can go in mandating platform-side content moderation, reinforcing Section 230 as a durable shield against state filtering mandates.
insights.locator: Texas cannot enforce a law's requirement

insights.claim: The 5th Circuit distinguished content-filtering mandates from age-verification mandates: it had previously upheld a Texas age-verification requirement for porn websites in 2024, but ruled that requiring platforms to monitor and filter content is 'all about filtering content' and therefore squarely preempted by Section 230's protection of publishing decisions.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Verification-style compliance duties (age gates, registration) survive legal challenge far more easily than content-moderation/filtering mandates -- a template for which state 'online safety' provisions are likely to be enforceable versus struck down.
insights.quote: monitoring and filtering requirement is all about filtering content, and is thus preempted

insights.claim: Despite blocking the filtering mandate, the court left most of the SCOPE Act intact because the plaintiff group challenging those other provisions lacked standing -- so Texas can still enforce age-registration requirements before account creation, bans on targeted ads to known minors, restrictions on ads for illegal products/activities aimed at minors, and mandatory 18+ age verification for platforms where more than one-third of content is obscene.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Platforms operating in Texas still face substantial compliance obligations around age gating and ad targeting even after this ruling -- it is a partial, not total, industry win.
insights.locator: Other parts of law can be enforced

insights.claim: The panel majority against the filtering mandate was formed by Reagan appointee Patrick Higginbotham and Biden appointee Dana Douglas, while Trump appointee James Ho dissented in part and argued the entire injunction should be upheld -- meaning the ruling did not split along the partisan lines one might expect from a court often described as conservative.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A cross-ideological judicial coalition on Section 230 preemption suggests the legal reasoning has broader durability than partisan-lean predictions of judicial outcomes would imply.

insights.claim: Dissenting judge James Ho argued the SCOPE Act should not be preempted because it regulates platforms' own curation algorithms -- which he calls the platforms' 'first-party speech' -- rather than the third-party content itself, distinguishing curation from publication.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: This curation-vs-publication framing is the emerging legal battleground for narrowing Section 230 and could resurface in other circuits or eventually the Supreme Court, keeping the litigation risk alive for platforms despite this loss for Texas.
insights.quote: The SCOPE Act isn’t preempted by section 230 for one simple reason: Because it regulates curation, not publication—first-party speech, not third-party speech.

insights.claim: Judge Ho cited Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas's view that social media platforms exploit the curation/third-party-content distinction inconsistently and self-servingly to turn Section 230 into a 'get-out-of-jail-free card,' signaling that at least one sitting Justice is skeptical of platforms' current Section 230 defenses.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Worth tracking whether the Supreme Court eventually takes up a circuit split on curation liability -- Thomas has already telegraphed an appetite to narrow Section 230's scope.

insights.claim: The 5th Circuit majority rejected the framing that platforms must choose between First Amendment editorial-discretion protection and Section 230 civil-liability protection, calling that a 'false choice' since the First Amendment shields platforms from direct government regulation of editorial decisions while Section 230 separately shields the same decisions from civil suits.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: This dual-protection doctrine (constitutional plus statutory) strengthens the legal defense platforms can deploy against future state content-moderation mandates beyond Texas.
insights.quote: The argument that we must choose between them presents a false choice.

insights.claim: Tech trade groups CCIA and NetChoice sued to block the SCOPE Act's monitoring/filtering provisions and won a preliminary injunction at the district court in August 2024; Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's appeal to the 5th Circuit failed to overturn that injunction.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Industry trade associations remain the primary legal vehicle blocking state child-safety internet laws -- their litigation docket is a leading indicator for which state tech regulations ultimately survive.

insights.claim: Paxton's losing argument was that the SCOPE Act 'imposes compliance duties, not publisher liability' and therefore aligns with rather than conflicts with Section 230's child-protection goals -- a framing the panel majority rejected.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: This 'compliance duty, not liability' argument is likely to resurface in other states' online-safety statutes; its rejection here previews it as a weak strategy specifically within the 5th Circuit.
insights.quote: imposes compliance duties, not publisher liability
insights.locator: Paxton argued that the Texas law imposes no liability

insights.claim: A student advocacy group, Students Engaged in Advancing Texas (SEAT), separately challenged the SCOPE Act on self-censorship and chilling-effect grounds, but all three judges unanimously found it lacked standing because the law does not apply directly to students and had not yet been enforced against platforms when the complaint was filed.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Pre-enforcement 'chilling effect' challenges to internet regulation face a high standing bar in the 5th Circuit -- a procedural hurdle that will slow future free-speech challenges to state tech laws and explains why parts of the SCOPE Act remain enforceable.

insights.claim: NetChoice publicly framed the ruling as protecting parental rather than governmental authority over children's online experience, calling the blocked filtering mandate an overbroad requirement that 'would have forced websites to censor broad, vaguely defined categories of lawful speech.'
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: This 'parents, not government' messaging is a reusable industry rhetoric template likely to reappear across other state litigation challenging online safety mandates.
insights.quote: would have forced websites to censor broad, vaguely defined categories of lawful speech
insights.locator: The law would have forced websites to censor

insights.claim: The 'famously conservative' 5th Circuit has a track record of upholding some Texas platform obligations -- including a 2024 age-verification mandate for porn websites -- while striking down others, showing the court draws its line specifically at content filtering/publisher-treatment rather than at platform regulation broadly.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The 5th Circuit's demonstrated willingness to uphold age-verification but not filtering mandates gives other states a legal template for drafting child-safety internet laws that are more likely to survive court challenge.
